blocks.markdown: **Covered persons**, natural or juridical, include: (1) BSP-supervised banks, non-banks, quasi-banks, trust entities, foreign exchange dealers, pawnshops, money changers, remittance and transfer companies and similar entities, with subsidiaries and affiliates; (2) IC-supervised insurance and pre-need companies and similar persons; (3) SEC-supervised securities dealers, brokers, salesmen, investment houses, mutual funds, close-end investment companies, common trust funds, and entities dealing in currency, commodities, financial derivatives, valuable objects, cash substitutes and similar instruments; (4)–(5) jewelry dealers in precious metals and precious stones above ₱1,000,000 per transaction; (6) company service providers; and (7) persons providing client-money/asset management, account management, company-formation, and business-entity services. The 2021 amendment further includes **real estate developers and brokers, and offshore gaming operators and their service providers**; see the full current wording in RA 11521 and the January 2021 amended IRR.

In plain English: covered persons are entities or professionals with legal duties to **identify customers, keep records, monitor activity, and report transactions**. The list is wider than banks — it can include certain insurers, securities businesses, remitters, casinos, real-estate businesses, and designated non-financial businesses/professions.

The three central duties are **know-your-customer checks, record retention, and reporting**. Reporting a suspicious transaction does not itself mean the customer committed a crime; the report alerts the AMLC so it can evaluate the information.

Covered persons must **establish and record the true identity of clients based on official documents**, maintain a verification system, and for corporate clients verify legal existence, organizational structure, and the authority and identification of representatives. **Anonymous accounts, accounts under fictitious names, and similar accounts are absolutely prohibited**, subject to the statutory allowance for non-checking numbered accounts. The 2018 IRR, Rule 18, Section 3.1 restates the duty: identify and record the true identity of customers, whether permanent or occasional, natural or juridical person, or legal arrangement. In plain English: know who is actually using the service, not merely the name typed into a form.

All records of all transactions must be **maintained and safely stored for five (5) years from the date of transactions**. For closed accounts, customer-identification records, account files, and business correspondence must be preserved for **at least five (5) years from closure**. In plain English: records must let investigators reconstruct who moved money, how much, when, and through which accounts; destroying or failing to keep required records can lead to liability.

Covered persons must report **all covered and suspicious transactions within five (5) working days from occurrence**, unless the Supervising Authority prescribes a longer period **not exceeding ten (10) working days**. A transaction that is both covered and suspicious is reported **as a suspicious transaction**. No administrative, criminal, or civil proceedings lie against a person who made a report in the regular performance of duties in good faith, whether or not prosecution follows; covered persons and their officers/employees must not **tip off** customers or others about the fact, contents, or related information of a report. In plain English: report in good faith through the prescribed process, and do not warn the customer, since that could allow funds or evidence to be moved.
**Glossary — CTR / STR:** covered-transaction report / suspicious-transaction report. A good-faith report is protected; tipping-off is prohibited.
